answer: As ferramentas MCP (Model Context Protocol) funcionam como parte de um padrão aberto que permite que aplicações de IA se conectem a diversas ferramentas e fontes de dados de maneira uniforme. Antes do MCP, cada integração entre uma aplicação e uma API era feita de forma personalizada e manual. Com o MCP, existe um protocolo comum que possibilita que um único cliente (aplicação de IA) se comunique com múltiplos servidores (ferramentas ou fontes de dados) intercambiáveis, facilitando a interoperabilidade e padronizando essas conexões. Isso torna o uso e a integração de ferramentas muito mais simples e escaláveis para aplicações de IA.

chunks.text:
An **MCP server** exposes capabilities — most importantly *tools* (functions the
model can call), but also *resources* (readable data) and *prompts* (reusable
templates). An **MCP client**, embedded in the AI application, connects to one
or more servers, discovers what they offer, and exposes those tools to the
agent. Communication happens over a transport such as stdio (for local servers
launched as subprocesses) or HTTP/SSE (for remote servers).
chunks.title: Model Context Protocol (MCP)

chunks.text: # Model Context Protocol (MCP)
chunks.title: Model Context Protocol (MCP)

chunks.text:
The Model Context Protocol is an open standard that lets AI applications connect
to tools and data sources in a uniform way. Before MCP, every integration was
bespoke: each app wired up each API by hand. MCP defines a common protocol so a
single client can talk to many interchangeable servers.
chunks.title: Model Context Protocol (MCP)

chunks.text:
The handshake is what makes MCP powerful. When a client connects, it asks the
server to list its tools. Each tool comes with a name, a human-readable
description, and a JSON schema describing its arguments. The agent uses these
descriptions to decide which tool to call and how to fill in the arguments. When
the agent calls a tool, the client forwards the request to the server, the
server runs it, and the result flows back to the model.
chunks.title: Model Context Protocol (MCP)

chunks.text:
Because the interface is standardized, the same MCP server can be reused across
different agents and frameworks. This decoupling is the main benefit: tools and
agents evolve independently, and adding a capability is as simple as connecting
another server.
chunks.title: Model Context Protocol (MCP)

chunks.text:
The most common pattern is **ReAct** (Reason + Act). On each turn the model
either emits a tool call (an action) or a final answer. When it emits a tool
call, the orchestrator runs the tool and feeds the result back into the
conversation, then asks the model again. The loop continues until the model
decides to answer or a step limit is reached. The step limit is important: it
prevents runaway loops and bounds cost and latency.
chunks.title: AI Agents and the ReAct Loop
chunks.section: AI Agents and the ReAct Loop

chunks.text:
# Prompt Engineering

A prompt is the full input given to a language model, and its structure
strongly shapes the output. Most production prompts are assembled from several
parts: a **system message** that sets the model's role and rules, the retrieved
**context** from RAG, the **conversation history**, any **tool results**, and
finally the user's current message. Understanding what actually gets sent is one
of the most useful debugging skills in AI engineering.
chunks.title: Prompt Engineering

chunks.text:
Good agent design is mostly about constraints: a clear system prompt, a small
set of well-described tools, and sensible limits. Too many tools confuse the
model; vague tool descriptions lead to wrong calls. The art is giving the model
just enough freedom to be useful without letting it wander.
chunks.title: AI Agents and the ReAct Loop
chunks.section: AI Agents and the ReAct Loop

chunks.text:
Frameworks like LangGraph model this loop as a graph of nodes. A typical graph
has a node that calls the model, a conditional edge that checks whether the
model requested a tool, a tool-execution node, and an edge that loops back to
the model node. Modeling the agent as an explicit state machine makes it easy to
add memory, branching, retries, and human-in-the-loop checkpoints.
chunks.title: AI Agents and the ReAct Loop
chunks.section: AI Agents and the ReAct Loop

chunks.text:
Prompt engineering is iterative. Small wording changes can have outsized effects,
so it pays to inspect the assembled prompt, change one thing at a time, and
evaluate against real examples. The prompt is not an afterthought; it is part of
the system's logic.
chunks.title: Prompt Engineering

chunks.text:
The Model Context Protocol is an open standard that lets AI applications connect
to tools and data sources in a uniform way. Before MCP, every integration was
bespoke: each app wired up each API by hand. MCP defines a common protocol so a
single client can talk to many interchangeable servers.

chunks.text:

chunks.text:

different agents and frameworks. This decoupling is the main benefit: tools and
agents evolve independently, and adding a capability is as simple as connecting
another server.
chunks.title: Model Context Protocol (MCP)

chunks.text:
Because models are stateless between calls, the application is responsible for
managing context: deciding what history to keep, what to retrieve, and what to
drop when the window fills up. Managing the context window well is a core part
of building reliable LLM applications.

chunks.text:

server to list its tools. Each tool comes with a name, a human-readable

the agent calls a tool, the client forwards the request to the server, the
server runs it, and the result flows back to the model.
chunks.title: Model Context Protocol (MCP)

chunks.text:
The system message is where you encode behavior: the persona, the tone, hard
constraints, and instructions about how to use the provided context. A good
system prompt tells the model to ground its answers in the retrieved context and
to say when it does not know, rather than inventing facts.
chunks.title: Prompt Engineering

chunks.text:
# Prompt Engineering

A prompt is the full input given to a language model, and its structure

of the most useful debugging skills in AI engineering.

chunks.text:
Order and formatting matter. Models pay more attention to the beginning and end
of a long prompt, so the most important instructions belong there. Clear
delimiters — headings, fenced blocks, labels like "Retrieved context" — help the
model separate instructions from data and reduce the chance it confuses the two.

args.content:
O Model Context Protocol (MCP) é um padrão aberto que permite que aplicações de IA se conectem a ferramentas e fontes de dados de forma uniforme. Antes do MCP, cada integração era feita sob medida, com cada aplicativo conectando manualmente cada API. O MCP define um protocolo comum para que um único cliente possa se comunicar com muitos servidores intercambiáveis.

Ainda não há detalhes específicos sobre o funcionamento das ferramentas MCP, mas o protocolo em si facilita a interoperabilidade e a padronização das conexões entre aplicações de IA e suas ferramentas associadas.

data.answer: As ferramentas MCP (Model Context Protocol) funcionam como parte de um padrão aberto que permite que aplicações de IA se conectem a diversas ferramentas e fontes de dados de maneira uniforme. Antes do MCP, cada integração entre uma aplicação e uma API era feita de forma personalizada e manual. Com o MCP, existe um protocolo comum que possibilita que um único cliente (aplicação de IA) se comunique com múltiplos servidores (ferramentas ou fontes de dados) intercambiáveis, facilitando a interoperabilidade e padronizando essas conexões. Isso torna o uso e a integração de ferramentas muito mais simples e escaláveis para aplicações de IA.
